title: Prototype Testing & Validation
summary: Prototype tiers, DVP-R test planning, instrumentation basics, Weibull reliability, and sample-size logic for design validation.

sections.heading: Validate Before You Commit
sections.content: Prototyping validates the design against reality **before** tooling money is spent — the cheapest place to find errors is before the die, mold, or production line exists. Validation is a discipline with a structure: build the right *tier* of prototype, test the right *characteristics*, with enough *samples* to believe the result, and record everything in a **DVP-R** so the evidence survives the project. A validation story is what turns a design into a release (see [[engineering-specifications|specifications]] for what "pass" means).

sections.heading: Prototype Tiers
sections.content:
Match the prototype to the question being asked:

| Tier | Purpose | Typical fabrication |
|---|---|---|
| Looks-like | Form, ergonomics, styling | 3D print, foam, SLA (see [[additive-manufacturing|AM]]) |
| Works-like (breadboard) | Function alone, not final form | Machined, bench rigs, off-shelf parts |
| Engineering (alpha) | Function + form, near-final materials | Machined/printed to final tolerances |
| Production-intent (beta) | Final process validation | Soft tooling, pilot production line |

Critical discipline: **functional or physical validation must use production-equivalent materials and processes** — a 3D-printed nylon bracket tells you nothing about the fatigue life of the die-cast aluminium production part ([[casting-forging-and-molding|casting]] properties and AM anisotropy differ completely). Use looks-like for appearance, works-like for physics, engineering prototypes for the actual design release.

sections.heading: The DVP-R: Design Verification Plan
sections.content:
The **DVP-R** is the test specification — the only document that makes validation auditable:

1. **Item** — the component/assembly and which spec it verifies.
2. **Test method & standard** — the procedure (ISO/ASTM derivative or internal), test rig, and fixture.
3. **Conditions** — load, temperature, cycles, media, orientation, duration.
4. **Acceptance criteria** — the numbers from the spec sheet (see [[engineering-specifications|specs]]).
5. **Sample size & justification** — how many units and why (statistics below).
6. **Result & status** — pass/fail with data, photo/plot evidence, and sign-off.

The DVP-R is fed by the **FMEA** (failure modes & effects analysis): each credible failure mode with high Severity × Occurrence × Detection becomes a test line. If the FMEA says "it could crack" and the DVP has no test for it, the risk is unmanaged—not absent.

sections.heading: Test Families
sections.content:
Validation tests map to the physics of the part:

- **Functional** — does it do the job: torque output, flow rate, force, speed, efficiency.
- **Structural** — strength and stiffness: 3-point bending, tensile, crush, proof load; compare to FEA prediction (see [[cae-analysis|CAE]]) — the model-vs-test correlation is the real validation product.
- **Environmental** — thermal cycling, humidity, salt spray (corrosion), UV, dust/water ingress (IP ratings), chemical exposure.
- **Dynamic** — vibration (sine sweep, random PSD), shock, drop; resonance search finds the natural frequencies FEA predicted.
- **Life/fatigue** — accelerated cycling to the endurance requirement (see [[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|fatigue]]): run to failure or to proof of life.
- **EMC/electrical** for electromechanical products; **ergonomics/human factors** for anything people operate.

Plan the sequence to fail fast: functional first (cheapest), structural and life next (most information per dollar), environmental last (longest, most expensive).

sections.heading: Instrumentation & Data
sections.content:
A test rig without instrumentation is theater; instrumentation choices decide what you learn:

- **Load cells / torque transducers** — force and torque at the actuation; calibrate before and after each run.
- **Strain gauges** — the measuring tool for stress: bond to the highest-strain location (from FEA), quarter/half/full bridges, temperature-compensated. Converts to stress via $\sigma = E \varepsilon$.
- **Accelerometers** — vibration and resonance; ICP (charge) types for rugged environments; mount rigidly, avoid cable whipping artifacts.
- **Thermocouples / RTDs** — temperature at critical points; type K for general, calibrated against a reference.
- **DAQ and sampling** — sample ≥ 10× the highest frequency of interest (Nyquist + margin); record raw + the derived channel; log metadata (serial numbers, conditions, operator).

The output is a **correlated dataset**: measured stress vs FEA stress, resonance vs simulation — this is the moment CAE earns trust for the next design iteration.

sections.heading: Sample Size & Confidence
sections.content:
How many prototypes prove the point? Statistics decide — the **Weibull** distribution models life data:

$$R(t) = e^{-(t/\eta)^\beta}$$

($\eta$ characteristic life, $\beta$ shape: <1 infant mortality, =1 random failure, >1 wearout.) For the common "demonstrate reliability R with confidence C with zero failures" case, the binomial relation $C = 1 - R^n$ inverts to:

$$n = \frac{\ln(1-C)}{\ln(R)}$$

Demo **90% reliability at 90% confidence, zero failures**: $n = \ln(0.10)/\ln(0.90) = 21.85 \to 22$ samples. Demo 95/90 → 45 samples. Fewer samples with failures need order-statistics tables (Weibayes/rank regression): 2 failures allowed → ~45 samples at 90/90. The uncomfortable truth: "we tested one unit, it passed" proves almost nothing about reliability — sample size is a calculable requirement, not a budget choice. Feed failures back into the design loop ([[fatigue-and-failure-analysis|failure analysis]]) and re-test to closure.

sections.heading: Test Report & Design Freeze
sections.content:
Validation closes with a **design freeze**, not an opinion:

- The test report tabulates every DVP-R line: result, evidence, deviation, and disposition (pass / conditional / fail-and-redesign).
- **Conditional passes** get documented with the exact conditions and a deadline; silent "it probably holds" is not a disposition.
- The freeze releases the design for tooling and production (see [[manufacturing-process-selection|process selection]]) with the validation evidence attached — the ECO includes test results as its justification (see [[engineering-drawings-and-bom|change control]]).
- Production then re-validates: first-article inspection ([[metrology-and-inspection|metrology]]), SPC capability ([[quality-control-and-spc|SPC]]), and any process-qualification tests — closing the loop from specification to ship.

A defensible product has a chain: spec → FMEA → DVP-R → test results → freeze. Every link documented, every deviation explained. That chain is what survives the audit, the lawsuit, and the field failure review.

keyTakeaways: Match the prototype tier to the question: looks-like for form, works-like for physics, production-intent for the final process.
DVP-R + FMEA link every credible failure mode to a test with acceptance criteria.
Instrument to learn: strain gauges, load cells, accelerometers — sampled ≥10× the highest frequency of interest.
Zero-failure demo of 90% reliability at 90% confidence needs 22 samples: n = ln(1−C)/ln(R).
